description: The inner ear begins as a thickened patch of surface ectoderm, the otic placode, which invaginates and pinches off to form the otic vesicle; otic vesicle formation is that transition, and everything downstream depends on it. The vesicle is the transient epithelial sac from which the cochlea, vestibular organs, endolymphatic duct and the sensory hair cells and neurons of the auditory-vestibular system are later patterned, so disruption at this stage produces profound congenital deafness and balance defects. Fibroblast growth factor signalling through FGF8 and FGF10 acting on FGFR2 induces and shapes the placode, while transcription factors including SOX9, PROX1 and HESX1 drive the epithelial morphogenesis and regional identity that make closure possible. Ciliary and structural contributions, such as CEP290, link this morphogenesis to broader syndromic disorders in which hearing loss accompanies retinal and renal disease.

Endoderm is the germ layer that gives rise to gut, liver, pancreas and lung epithelium, and the differentiation of cells into it must be timed and positioned correctly during gastrulation or organ primordia form in the wrong place or not at all. The genes here act as modulators rather than core effectors of that fate decision: a secreted Wnt antagonist tunes the Wnt/nodal signalling gradients that partition mesoderm from endoderm, a bHLH transcription factor of the nascent mesoderm helps set the boundary between the two lineages, a histone variant that marks facultative heterochromatin constrains which lineage programmes remain accessible, and fibrillar collagen V contributes to the extracellular matrix through which migrating cells receive positional cues. Together they illustrate how signalling, chromatin state and matrix context converge to raise or lower the rate at which cells adopt endodermal identity.

Somitogenesis carves the presomitic mesoderm into paired blocks that later give rise to vertebrae, ribs, skeletal muscle and dermis, and this set concerns the inputs that set how fast and how regularly those segments form. Notch signalling supplies the oscillatory clock: the ligand DLL1 and receptor NOTCH1 couple neighbouring cells, while the glycosyltransferase LFNG modifies Notch to modulate ligand sensitivity and keep the oscillation periodic and phase-locked across the field. Caudal-type homeobox factors CDX1 and CDX2 pattern posterior axial identity and maintain the progenitor pool from which new somites are added, and DMRT2 acts in the forming somite to fix segment polarity and myogenic competence. Disturbance of this timing produces irregular, fused or asymmetric segments, the developmental basis of congenital vertebral malformations such as spondylocostal dysostosis.

Specification of the secondary heart field sets aside a pool of lateral mesoderm distinct from the first heart field, and its descendants build most of the right ventricle together with the outflow tract at the arterial pole and part of the inflow tract at the venous pole. Because these are precisely the structures malformed in conotruncal and right-heart congenital heart disease, the delineation step underlies tetralogy of Fallot, double-outlet right ventricle and persistent truncus arteriosus. Mesodermal progenitors marked by MESP1 are directed into this territory by BMP4 and by non-canonical WNT5A and WNT11 signalling, with canonical Wnt output tuned through AXIN2 and Notch input relayed by RBPJ. ISL1 identifies the undifferentiated progenitor state, while MEF2C and the chromatin-remodelling subunit SMARCD3 drive the transcriptional programme that commits these cells to cardiomyocyte fate and later cardiac morphogenesis.

The kidney begins when an outgrowth emerges from the Wolffian duct toward the metanephric mesenchyme; ureteric bud formation covers that first protrusion, from the moment epithelium bulges out of the duct until a distinct bud exists. Everything downstream depends on it — the bud branches into the collecting duct system and its tips induce nephron progenitors, so failure or ectopic budding produces renal agenesis, hypoplasia, duplex kidneys and vesicoureteric reflux. Mesenchymal GDNF is the inductive signal, its production controlled by SIX1 and SIX4 and its reception restricted in position by GATA3 within the duct epithelium. Sulfation of heparan sulfate by HS2ST1 shapes how that signal is presented, while BMP antagonists such as GREM1 and NOG relieve BMP4 inhibition so that budding occurs at one site and one time.

Each somite is polarised into rostral and caudal halves before any morphological boundary appears, and this patterning is what later dictates where sclerotome cells condense, where vertebrae segment relative to muscle, and along which corridor migrating neural crest cells and motor axons may travel. Loss of the polarity produces fused and malformed vertebrae and disordered spinal nerve segmentation, as seen in congenital spine disorders. The bHLH factors MESP1 and MESP2 are induced in the rostral presomitic mesoderm as segmentation clock and Notch signals converge, with TBX6 licensing their expression and NRARP tuning Notch output; RIPPLY1 and RIPPLY2 then feed back to extinguish TBX6 and MESP activity, sharpening the boundary. LHX1 and nodal-type signalling through GDF3 and SMAD4 contribute upstream, while EPB41L5 links the resulting polarity to epithelialisation of the forming somite.

Some tubes in the body are not built by wrapping cells around a space but by hollowing out an already solid cord of cells, and tube lumen cavitation is that clearing step. It matters wherever a duct must connect a secretory organ to a surface: sweat and salivary glands, mammary ducts, and the airways all depend on converting a cord into a patent conduit, and failure leaves a blind or occluded duct with loss of secretion. Ectodysplasin signalling through its receptor drives the process in skin appendage ducts, and mutations in this ligand-receptor pair cause hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia, in which sweat glands fail to form usable lumens. Hedgehog signalling and an NFI-family transcription factor supply epithelial patterning and branching context, while transglutaminase activity remodels the surrounding matrix. The step links epithelial morphogenesis to programmed cell clearance and cell rearrangement.

Epithelial tubes are the structural basis of kidney nephrons, airways, glands and blood vessels, and this pathway covers the signals that promote their formation rather than the tube-building itself. Growth factors dominate: GDNF drives ureteric bud outgrowth and branching in kidney development, while EGF, FGF2 and VEGFA stimulate epithelial and endothelial cells to proliferate, migrate and organise into lumenised cords. These cues converge on intracellular signalling, with PI3K catalytic subunits relaying receptor activation to cytoskeletal and survival responses. Transcription factors act upstream and in parallel: SIX1 and SIX4 specify nephrogenic mesenchyme and sustain GDNF expression, and GATA3 is required for ureteric epithelium identity. Matrix components such as MMRN2 contribute to the extracellular environment guiding tube formation. Loss of these inputs causes renal agenesis or hypoplasia, branchio-oto-renal syndrome, and defective vascular and glandular tubulogenesis.

Acrosome assembly is the step in spermiogenesis that converts Golgi-derived proacrosomal vesicles into the single large cap covering the anterior sperm nucleus, the secretory organelle whose hydrolases and adhesion proteins let a sperm penetrate the zona pellucida and fuse with the egg. Without it spermatozoa are globozoospermic — round-headed, acrosome-less and infertile — a recognised cause of male infertility treatable only by assisted fertilisation. The genes here cover vesicle trafficking and tethering from the Golgi, a Rab GAP and Golgi-associated tethering factors, membrane fusion and docking, and the acroplaxome/acrosome–acroplaxome anchoring machinery built on actin-related proteins that also couples the acrosome to nuclear shaping and manchette function. Transcriptional regulators active in round spermatids drive the haploid programme, while zona-binding and sperm–egg interaction proteins are the cargo whose correct packaging is the point of the whole process.

Oligodendrocytes in the brain and spinal cord extend processes that spiral around axons and compact their membrane into myelin, the insulating sheath that permits fast saltatory conduction and supports long-term axonal integrity. Central nervous system myelin formation sets conduction velocity in white matter tracts, and its failure or breakdown underlies leukodystrophies and demyelinating disease such as multiple sclerosis. The genes here act at several stages: recognition and adhesion between the glial membrane and the axon surface through myelin-associated glycoprotein and contactin, lipid handling and intracellular trafficking needed to build a membrane of unusual composition, and regulators that control oligodendrocyte differentiation and process outgrowth. The pathway therefore links glial cell fate and membrane biogenesis to axon-glia communication, and connects to broader programmes of neural development and white matter maintenance.

During gastrulation, epiblast cells must decide whether to become mesoderm, and this regulatory layer sets how many do so, where, and when. The outcome determines the heart, blood, skeleton and muscle that later derive from mesoderm, and misregulation produces axis duplication, failed primitive streak formation or absent cardiac progenitors. Control is exerted largely by extracellular signals and their tuning: WNT3A drives streak formation while the secreted antagonists DKK1 and SFRP2 restrain WNT signalling to limit the mesodermal domain, BMP receptor signalling through BMPR1A patterns posterior and extraembryonic mesoderm, and FGFR1 is required for cells to ingress through the streak and adopt mesodermal identity. Downstream, the transcription factor MESP1 marks and specifies nascent cardiovascular mesoderm. The same signalling logic is exploited to steer pluripotent stem cells toward mesodermal lineages in culture.

Neural fold formation is the shaping step that converts the flat neural plate into a U-shaped groove: the plate edges thicken and elevate, bringing the prospective dorsal margins toward each other so that they can later fuse into the neural tube. Without it, closure fails and the result is a neural tube defect such as exencephaly, anencephaly or spina bifida. The genes here span the signals and the machinery that execute the bending. BMP family ligands and NODAL provide dorsoventral patterning cues from surrounding tissue, while cofilin-mediated actin filament severing and other cytoskeletal regulators generate the apical constriction and cell shape changes that hinge the epithelium. A chromatin remodelling component and transcriptional regulators couple these signals to gene expression in surface ectoderm and neuroepithelium, linking morphogenesis to the patterning of the early central nervous system.

Endodermal cell fate specification is the step at which a cell in the early embryo becomes competent to differentiate into endoderm on its own, though the commitment is still reversible and can be overridden by other signals. It sets aside the germ layer that gives rise to gut epithelium, liver, pancreas, lung and thyroid, so failures here compromise the entire digestive and respiratory lineage, and the same programme is exploited to make definitive endoderm from pluripotent stem cells in culture. Pluripotency factors such as POU5F1 and NANOG provide the starting state, SOX2 must be extinguished as SOX17 comes on, and EOMES acts with nodal signalling to drive endoderm rather than mesoderm, an alternative marked by MESP1. HNF1B carries the decision forward into gut tube patterning, while DKK1 antagonises Wnt to bias regional identity.

Cardiac myofibril assembly builds the ordered sarcomeric apparatus that lets heart muscle cells contract, taking nascent actin bundles in the developing myocardium through to mature, aligned myofibrils. Without it the embryonic heart cannot generate organized force, and in the adult heart defective assembly or maintenance of sarcomeric components underlies dilated and hypertrophic cardiomyopathies. Cardiac actin and the ventricular myosin light chain supply the contractile core, while titin acts as the molecular ruler spanning the sarcomere and telethonin anchors its Z-disc end; formin-family FHOD3 and nebulin-related proteins organize and length-regulate the thin filaments, and myosin light chain kinase 3 tunes contractility. Z-disc proteins such as CSRP3 couple mechanical strain to signalling. Transcriptional inputs from NKX2-5, SRF, PROX1 and SMAD4, together with PDGF receptor signalling, link cardiomyocyte differentiation and growth cues to the sarcomeric gene programme.

Trachea formation covers the earliest events that carve a single cartilage-supported airway tube out of the anterior foregut, separating it from the esophagus and connecting it to the branching bronchi below. Getting this right determines whether an infant can breathe and swallow independently; failure produces tracheoesophageal fistula, esophageal atresia, tracheal agenesis or stenosis, and the tracheomalacia seen when the cartilage rings are malformed. The genes involved place the process at the intersection of BMP and TGF-beta signalling from the surrounding splanchnic mesenchyme, canonical Wnt signalling through beta-catenin in the foregut endoderm, and the MEK1/MEK2-ERK1/ERK2 kinase cascade that relays growth factor input into proliferation and dorsoventral patterning of the tube. Epithelial-mesenchymal crosstalk of this kind decides where respiratory identity begins and where cartilage and smooth muscle differentiate around it.

Somite specification is the step in vertebrate trunk development at which each newly formed block of paraxial mesoderm acquires its own positional and segmental identity, fixing which vertebra, rib and body-wall muscle group will derive from it. Getting this wrong produces fused or malformed vertebrae and rib defects of the kind seen in congenital segmentation disorders of the spine. The genes here act at the boundary between the segmentation clock and stable somite patterning: Notch ligand signalling through DLL1 provides the oscillatory and boundary-forming cue, RIPPLY1 acts as a repressor that terminates that cue and sharpens the rostral-caudal subdivision of each somite, and the MEOX transcription factors specify sclerotome and dermomyotome fates within the segment. The pathway therefore links periodic patterning of the presomitic mesoderm to the axial skeleton and skeletal muscle that later form from it.

Skeletal muscle contracts only if its actin-based thin filaments are built to a defined length and anchored correctly within each sarcomere, and this assembly programme is what produces them. Skeletal alpha-actin polymerises into the filament core, with cardiac actin contributing in developing and regenerating fibres; leiomodin-3 nucleates new actin filaments and sets thin filament length, and its loss causes nemaline myopathy with disorganised, rod-containing fibres and severe congenital weakness. Titin spans the sarcomere as a molecular ruler and elastic element, and telethonin binds its Z-disc end to help anchor the filament lattice. The transcription factor PROX1 contributes to the myogenic gene programme that establishes fibre-type-appropriate sarcomeric components. Together these activities link myofibrillogenesis during muscle development and repair to the force-generating geometry that thick-thin filament sliding requires.

Organs do not arise from single cells acting alone; they form where one tissue signals to a neighbour and changes its fate. Organ induction describes these reciprocal interactions, typically between epithelium and adjacent mesenchyme, that commit a field of cells to build a kidney, limb, lung, heart or gonad. The signalling currencies are few and reused: fibroblast growth factors and their receptor and adaptor components, bone morphogenetic proteins, and WNT ligands acting through beta-catenin, with DKK1 and SPRY1 restraining WNT and FGF output so induction stays spatially bounded. Transcription factors such as SIX1, GATA5, MESP1 and posterior HOX proteins read these cues and fix regional identity, while GDNF-driven signalling initiates ureteric branching. Loss or misplacement of these inductive signals produces organ agenesis, hypoplasia and congenital malformation, linking the pathway to embryonic patterning and branching morphogenesis.

The prostate begins as buds of epithelium that emerge from the fetal urogenital sinus, and this pathway covers the signals that set how many buds form, where, and how far they grow. Androgen receptor signalling in the surrounding mesenchyme licenses budding in males, and the epithelial-mesenchymal dialogue that follows determines prostate size and branching architecture; failure of these controls gives prostatic agenesis or hypoplasia, while the same signalling axes are reactivated in benign hyperplasia and prostate cancer. Hedgehog signalling from the budding epithelium and WNT5A from mesenchyme position and restrain outgrowth, BMP4 and BMP7 act largely as inhibitors that limit bud number, and the extracellular sulfatase SULF1 tunes availability of heparan sulfate-bound growth factors. Together these define an androgen-dependent branching morphogenesis programme.

The nephric duct is the tube that drains the primitive kidney, and its initial formation sets up the plumbing from which the ureter, collecting system and, in males, parts of the reproductive tract derive. Epithelialisation of the intermediate mesoderm into a patent duct that extends caudally to insert into the cloaca depends on a small transcriptional and signalling module: PAX2 and GATA3 specify and maintain the nephric duct epithelium and guide its caudal extension, HNF1B shapes tubular epithelial identity, and BMP4 and WNT9B provide the surrounding instructive signals, with WNT9B later inducing metanephric mesenchyme. Failure or misrouting at this stage produces congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract, including renal agenesis, duplex or ectopic ureters and vesicoureteral reflux, and mutations in these regulators cause inherited renal-coloboma and renal cyst syndromes.

Vertebrate embryos build their trunk and tail progressively from a caudal progenitor zone, and axis elongation during somitogenesis is the growth that extends the head-to-tail axis so that successive somites can be laid down behind the advancing tail bud. Without it the axis is truncated, somite number is reduced, and the vertebrae, ribs and axial muscles derived from those segments are correspondingly incomplete. The genes here point to WNT signalling as the driver: WNT3A ligand from the posterior growth zone maintains presomitic mesoderm progenitors, SFRP1 sequesters Wnt ligands and NKD1 acts as an induced negative feedback regulator, tuning pathway output rather than simply switching it on. A Mediator complex subunit links the pathway to transcriptional output, and a protein phosphatase 2A regulatory subunit contributes phosphorylation-dependent control. The result couples posterior progenitor renewal to the segmentation clock that times somite formation.

Metanephric tubule formation is the step at which mesenchymal cells of the kidney-forming metanephros first organize into an epithelial tube, the precursor of the nephron's proximal tubule, loop and distal segments that will later filter and reabsorb from the blood. Failure of this step leaves nephrons unformed, producing renal hypoplasia, dysplasia or agenesis and the reduced nephron endowment that predisposes to later kidney disease. The paired box factors PAX2 and PAX8 act partly redundantly to specify and maintain the nephric epithelial state, SOX8 and SOX9 contribute transcriptional input to progenitor behaviour, and WNT9B from the ureteric epithelium induces WNT4 in surrounding cap mesenchyme, which drives mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition. The biology thus links inductive Wnt signalling between adjacent tissues to lineage specification and epithelial tube morphogenesis during organogenesis.

The second heart field is a pool of committed but still dividing cardiac precursors that supplies the right ventricle, the outflow tract and the inflow region, and how long those cardioblasts keep proliferating before differentiating sets the size of these structures. Control of that proliferative window matters clinically: too little expansion of the field underlies conotruncal and outflow tract malformations, including persistent truncus arteriosus and double outlet right ventricle, and contributes to hypoplasia of right-sided chambers. The regulators here combine progenitor identity with growth signalling — ISL1 marks the undifferentiated second heart field state, a SIX1–EYA1 transcriptional pair and the Notch effector HES1 restrain or sustain division, HAND2 and TBX5 pattern the cardiac lineage, and beta-catenin couples Wnt input to precursor expansion. The pathway thus sits at the junction of cardiac fate commitment and cell cycle control during cardiac morphogenesis.

Turning a flat epithelial sheet into a sealed tube — most consequentially the neural tube, but also the optic fissure and palate — requires the edges of an epithelial fold to bend, meet and fuse, creating the central lumen. Failure produces some of the commonest human birth defects: spina bifida, anencephaly and craniorachischisis, which is why folate metabolism genes such as MTHFR, MTHFD1 and the receptor FOLR1 sit alongside the morphogenetic machinery here. Closure depends on planar cell polarity components (VANGL2, CELSR1, PRICKLE1, FZD3/6, SCRIB) to drive convergent extension, on actin regulators such as PFN1, VASP and COBL to constrict apical surfaces, and on hedgehog, BMP and WNT signalling — with NOG and SFRPs as antagonists — to pattern the dorsal neuroepithelium. Ciliary and intraflagellar transport proteins tune that signalling, and apoptotic caspases remodel the fusing seam.

Paraxial mesoderm is the band of tissue flanking the neural tube that later segments into somites and gives rise to the axial skeleton, skeletal muscle and dermis, so its initial formation sets up the segmented body plan of the trunk. During gastrulation, cells emerging from the primitive streak must be allocated to a paraxial rather than lateral or intermediate fate, and Wnt ligands acting through canonical and non-canonical routes drive both that allocation and the collective movement of the cells into position; LEF1 transduces the canonical arm to target genes. The forkhead factors FOXC1 and FOXC2 act redundantly to maintain paraxial identity and subsequent somite formation, and their loss produces axial skeletal and vascular defects. Vesicle trafficking through the exocyst contributes the membrane delivery that polarized migration and convergent extension require.

Muscle cells generate force only when actin and myosin are packed into sarcomeres, the repeating contractile units bounded by Z discs, and this pathway covers the signals that promote and accelerate that assembly. It matters most in the heart, where myofibril growth accompanies cardiomyocyte maturation and the hypertrophic response to load; failure of sarcomere assembly and alignment underlies dilated cardiomyopathy and thin, poorly contractile ventricular walls. The genes here act as upstream instructions rather than structural components: a cardiac-restricted growth factor of the BMP family and the vasoactive peptide endothelin-1 act as paracrine cues, a myosin light chain kinase and a protein kinase C-related kinase phosphorylate targets that set filament assembly and Z-disc gene expression, a transcription factor contributes to chamber and conduction patterning, and a muscle-enriched microRNA tunes the output. Together they link extracellular signalling to the building of the contractile apparatus.

Saltatory conduction depends on a tight seal where the myelin sheath meets the axon at each end of a node of Ranvier, and paranodal junction assembly builds that seal. The septate-like contacts formed there anchor the myelin loops to the axolemma, separate the sodium channels clustered at the node from the potassium channels of the juxtaparanode, and act as a diffusion barrier for the periaxonal space. A neurexin-family axonal adhesion protein, CNTNAP1, partners with contactin to engage glial neurofascin, while a band 4.1-like protein links the complex to the underlying cytoskeleton and a tetraspanin contributes to membrane organization. Galactolipid synthesis by UGT8 and ether lipid synthesis by GNPAT supply the myelin lipids on which junction integrity depends. Disruption causes conduction slowing, disorganized nodes and severe congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy.
